title: DNA replication

sections.title: Copying a DNA molecule
sections.body: Before division, a cell copies its DNA so that descendants can receive genetic information. Helicase separates the strands, allowing each to act as a template. DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides. Each resulting DNA molecule contains one pre-existing strand and one newly assembled strand: replication is semiconservative. Complementary pairing supports fidelity, but errors can still occur and may require repair.
sections.pitfall: Semiconservative does not mean that every resulting strand is a mixture of old and new fragments.

sections.title: PCR and DNA separation
sections.body: The polymerase chain reaction amplifies a selected DNA region through repeated temperature cycles. Heating separates strands; cooling allows primers to bind; a heat-stable polymerase extends them. Primers help determine the region copied. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments according to their movement through a gel: smaller fragments generally move farther under comparable conditions. Matching selected DNA markers supports an identification hypothesis but does not mean every part of two genomes is identical.
sections.pitfall: PCR makes more copies of a selected region; electrophoresis separates fragments and does not itself copy them.

questions.prompt: After one round of semiconservative replication, what does each daughter DNA molecule contain?
questions.answer: One old strand and one new strand
distractors: Two old strands
Two new strands with the original molecule unchanged
Two strands each made from alternating old and new sections
questions.explanation: Each parental strand serves as the template for one new complementary strand.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the purposes of PCR and gel electrophoresis.
questions.answer: PCR amplifies a selected region of DNA.~Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments, allowing patterns or sizes to be compared.
questions.explanation: State what each technique does to the sample.

questions.prompt: An idealized PCR begins with 8 target molecules and doubles their number in every cycle. Calculate the number after 5 cycles and state why a real experiment may yield fewer.
questions.answer: 8 × 2⁵ = 256 target molecules.~Incomplete amplification or limited reagents can prevent perfect doubling.
questions.explanation: The number of cycles is an exponent, not a simple multiplier.

remaining: Core mechanisms are introduced. Add experimental interpretation of DNA profiles and HL directionality, leading and lagging strands, primers, fragments and ligase.

title: Protein synthesis

sections.title: Transcription
sections.body: Transcription produces an RNA molecule using one DNA strand as a template. RNA polymerase assembles complementary RNA nucleotides; RNA contains uracil rather than thymine. In a eukaryotic cell, transcription of nuclear genes occurs in the nucleus. A messenger RNA carries sequence information used in protein synthesis. The template strand and the coding strand are not interchangeable: the RNA is complementary to the template and resembles the coding strand with U in place of T.
sections.pitfall: Transcription makes RNA, not a polypeptide.

sections.title: Translation and the genetic code
sections.body: A ribosome reads successive three-base codons in messenger RNA. Transfer RNAs carry amino acids and have anticodons that pair with suitable codons. The ribosome links amino acids through peptide bonds. A start codon establishes a reading frame, and a stop codon signals termination rather than specifying another amino acid. The genetic code is degenerate because several codons can specify the same amino acid; a given codon is not normally a choice between several amino acids.
sections.pitfall: A codon is a triplet on messenger RNA; an anticodon is the matching triplet on transfer RNA.

questions.prompt: Which molecule is directly synthesized during transcription?
questions.answer: RNA
distractors: A polypeptide
A triglyceride
A second DNA double helix
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase uses a DNA template to make an RNA transcript.

questions.prompt: Explain how transfer RNA connects the nucleotide sequence of a message to an amino-acid sequence.
questions.answer: Its anticodon pairs with a complementary messenger-RNA codon.~It carries the corresponding amino acid to the ribosome, where the amino acid can be added to the polypeptide.
questions.explanation: Link recognition of the codon to delivery of the amino acid.

questions.prompt: A coding sequence contains 90 RNA bases from its start codon through its stop codon, inclusive. Assume no intervening stop and no RNA processing within this sequence. Determine the number of amino acids encoded.
questions.answer: 90/3 = 30 codons.~One is a stop codon and does not encode an amino acid, so the polypeptide contains 29 amino acids.
questions.explanation: Count codons first, then account for the terminating codon.

remaining: Add genetic-code-table practice, full molecular diagrams and HL RNA processing, regulation and translation details.

title: Mutations and gene editing

sections.title: Mutation and its consequences
sections.body: A substitution replaces a base, while an insertion or deletion changes sequence length. In a coding region, inserting or deleting a number of bases not divisible by three can shift the reading frame. A substitution may change an amino acid, introduce a stop codon or leave the amino-acid sequence unchanged because the code is degenerate. Mutations can result from copying errors or mutagens. They are not directed toward an organism's future needs and can have neutral, harmful or beneficial effects depending on context.
sections.pitfall: A mutation does not necessarily alter the protein, and a change that helps in one environment need not help in another.

sections.title: Somatic and germ-line changes
sections.body: A mutation in a somatic cell can affect that cell and its descendants within the body without being transmitted to offspring through gametes. A mutation in a lineage that contributes to gametes can be inherited by an offspring receiving the altered DNA. The distinction depends on which lineage is affected, not on whether the mutation is beneficial or harmful. Mutation provides new alleles; selection changes their representation through differences in survival and reproduction.
sections.pitfall: Not every mutation occurring in a parent is inherited by every child.

sections.title: Investigating genes and targeted editing
sections.body: A knockout disables a gene, allowing researchers to compare the resulting phenotype with a suitable control. The effect may depend on genetic background or compensation by other genes. In CRISPR–Cas9 editing, a guide RNA helps direct Cas9 to a matching DNA target, where cutting and subsequent repair can alter the sequence. Targeting is not the same as guaranteed perfect editing. Off-target changes, delivery and the distinction between somatic and heritable changes matter when evaluating an application.
sections.pitfall: A knockout phenotype does not always reveal a gene's only function, and editing is not inherently free of unintended effects.

questions.prompt: Which change in a coding region is most likely to shift the downstream reading frame?
questions.answer: Insertion of one nucleotide
distractors: Substitution of one nucleotide
Deletion of exactly one complete codon
Insertion of exactly two complete codons
questions.explanation: Adding one base changes the grouping of later triplets; whole-codon changes preserve the downstream frame.

questions.prompt: Explain why a mutation in a skin cell is not normally inherited by the person's offspring.
questions.answer: A skin cell belongs to a somatic lineage rather than the lineage producing gametes.~The offspring receives DNA through gametes, not from that skin cell.
questions.explanation: Trace the route of transmission rather than assuming all cells contribute DNA to offspring.

questions.prompt: A bacterial variant survives an antibiotic exposure. A student concludes that the antibiotic caused the exact beneficial mutation because the bacteria needed it. Evaluate the explanation.
questions.answer: Survival is consistent with selection favouring a resistant variant.~The relevant mutation may have existed before exposure, and mutations are not directed toward future need.~Timing and comparison evidence would be needed to establish when the variant arose.
questions.explanation: Separate the origin of variation from selection acting on it.

questions.prompt: Discuss why a targeted gene-editing method still requires controls and follow-up testing.
questions.answer: Target recognition can make an intended change more likely than untargeted alteration.~Repair outcomes or off-target changes can produce unintended effects.~Comparisons with appropriate controls and follow-up measurements are needed to evaluate the actual phenotype and safety of the application.
questions.explanation: Present both the benefit of targeting and its limitations. This is an educational evaluation, not a clinical recommendation.

remaining: Core mutations are introduced and an HL editing overview is available. Add required successful editing examples, ethical evaluation and conserved-sequence evidence before calling the topic complete.

title: Cell and nuclear division

sections.title: Mitosis and the cell cycle
sections.body: DNA replication occurs before mitosis, producing sister chromatids. During mitosis, duplicated chromosomes are organized and sister chromatids separate so that daughter nuclei receive corresponding chromosome sets. Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm and is distinct from nuclear division. The cell cycle includes preparation as well as division. Disruption of normal control can allow abnormal proliferation, but observing a dividing cell alone is not evidence of cancer.
sections.pitfall: DNA is normally replicated before mitosis, not between every visible mitotic stage.

sections.title: Meiosis and chromosome number
sections.body: Meiosis follows one replication of DNA with two nuclear divisions. Homologous chromosomes separate in the first division and sister chromatids in the second, reducing the chromosome number. Crossing over and independent orientation can create new combinations of alleles. Fusion of haploid gametes restores a diploid chromosome number. Chromosome number and DNA quantity must be distinguished: replication increases DNA quantity without immediately doubling the number of centromere-defined chromosomes.
sections.pitfall: A replicated chromosome with two sister chromatids is not automatically counted as two separate chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Which structures normally separate from one another during the first meiotic division?
questions.answer: Homologous chromosomes
distractors: The two strands within every DNA double helix
All sister chromatids as in mitosis
Individual bases from their sugar–phosphate backbones
questions.explanation: Homologues separate in meiosis I; sister chromatids usually remain joined until meiosis II.

questions.prompt: Distinguish mitosis from cytokinesis.
questions.answer: Mitosis separates chromosome sets into daughter nuclei.~Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm into daughter cells.
questions.explanation: They are coordinated processes but describe different cellular events.

questions.prompt: A tissue sample contains 240 visible cells, of which 36 are in mitosis. Calculate the mitotic index as a percentage and state one limitation of comparing it with a different tissue.
questions.answer: 36/240 × 100 = 15%.~Different tissue functions or cell-cycle durations may affect the fraction in mitosis, so a higher index alone does not identify its cause.
questions.explanation: A snapshot fraction is not automatically a direct measurement of the rate at which all cells divide.

remaining: Add annotated stage identification, cytokinesis mechanisms, chromosome behaviour investigations and HL cell-cycle regulation.

title: Gene expression

sections.title: Regulating gene activity
sections.body: Gene expression can be controlled at transcription, RNA processing, translation and protein activity. Regulatory proteins can affect whether transcription proceeds. Different cell types express different combinations of genes, supporting specialization without requiring each type to possess an entirely different genome. Environmental signals can change expression, but a measured RNA concentration reflects both synthesis and degradation rather than transcription alone.
sections.pitfall: More messenger RNA does not guarantee a proportional increase in active protein.

sections.title: Chromatin and persistent changes
sections.body: Chemical modifications to DNA or associated proteins can change the accessibility of genes without changing the base sequence. DNA methylation is often associated with reduced expression in a context-dependent way. Some regulatory states persist through cell division. Epigenetic effects should be distinguished from sequence mutations, and persistence within a cell lineage should not automatically be described as inheritance through many generations of whole organisms.
sections.pitfall: A change in gene activity is not necessarily a change in the genetic code or DNA sequence.

questions.prompt: Which observation is consistent with epigenetic regulation rather than a base substitution?
questions.answer: Gene activity changes while the DNA base sequence remains unchanged
distractors: One base is replaced by a different base
A coding exon loses one nucleotide
A gene gains an extra coding triplet
questions.explanation: Epigenetic regulation can affect expression without altering the underlying sequence.

questions.prompt: Explain why measuring only messenger RNA may be insufficient to determine the amount of active protein.
questions.answer: Translation rate and protein degradation can vary independently of messenger-RNA abundance.~The protein may also require modification or activation before functioning.
questions.explanation: Expression is regulated at several stages, not only transcription.

questions.prompt: After a treatment, messenger-RNA abundance doubles, but protein abundance remains unchanged. Does this disprove regulation of gene expression? Explain.
questions.answer: No: the RNA observation is itself consistent with altered expression or RNA stability.~Translational regulation, protein turnover or the timing of measurement could explain the unchanged protein level.
questions.explanation: Different measured stages can respond differently and on different timescales.

remaining: Add the required regulatory examples, environmental effects and detailed experimental evidence. All resources in this topic are HL-only.

title: Water potential

sections.title: Osmosis and cell responses
sections.body: Across a membrane permeable to water but not the relevant solute, water moves net from the less concentrated solution toward the more concentrated solution when pressure conditions are comparable. This is osmosis. In an isotonic situation there is no net movement, but water molecules continue crossing both ways. Animal cells can swell and burst in a sufficiently hypotonic medium or shrink in a hypertonic one. Plant cell walls resist expansion, allowing turgor; strong water loss can cause the membrane to pull away from the wall in plasmolysis.
sections.pitfall: No net movement does not mean that individual water molecules stop moving.

sections.title: Investigating water movement
sections.body: Tissue pieces can be placed in different solute concentrations and weighed before and after a controlled interval. Percentage mass change allows comparison of pieces with different initial masses. A graph crossing zero change estimates an isotonic concentration under the experimental conditions. Control tissue source, size, temperature and immersion time; blot consistently before weighing. Repeated samples reveal biological variation. An estimate from a whole tissue is not an exact measurement of every cell's contents.
sections.pitfall: Residual surface solution can falsely increase the final mass and obscure the effect of osmosis.

sections.title: Calculating water potential
sections.body: Water potential describes the tendency of water to move relative to a reference state. Water moves net from higher toward lower water potential. In a simple cell model, Ψw = Ψs + Ψp: water potential equals solute potential plus pressure potential. Adding solute makes Ψs more negative. Positive pressure can offset that effect; tension can make pressure potential negative. Compare total potentials rather than solute concentrations alone when pressures differ.
sections.pitfall: A more negative number is a lower water potential; −200 kPa is higher than −400 kPa.

questions.prompt: What happens to water molecules in an isotonic situation across a water-permeable membrane?
questions.answer: They continue moving both ways with no net movement
distractors: They stop moving entirely
They move only into the cell
They can cross only if ATP is directly supplied
questions.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium describes balanced opposing movements.

questions.prompt: Explain why a plant cell can become turgid without bursting as readily as an animal cell.
questions.answer: Water enters and increases the volume and internal pressure.~The cell wall resists expansion and supports the developing pressure.
questions.explanation: The wall provides mechanical resistance; it does not prevent all water entry.

questions.prompt: A tissue piece increases in mass from 2.40 g to 2.58 g. Calculate its percentage mass change and suggest the net direction of water movement.
questions.answer: Percentage change = (2.58 − 2.40)/2.40 × 100 = +7.5%.~Net water entry is consistent with the mass increase if other mass changes are negligible.
questions.explanation: Use initial mass in the denominator and retain the sign.

questions.prompt: A cell has Ψs = −700 kPa and Ψp = +300 kPa. Its surroundings have Ψw = −200 kPa. Calculate the cell's water potential and determine the initial net direction of water movement.
questions.answer: Cell Ψw = −700 + 300 = −400 kPa.~Water initially moves from the surroundings at −200 kPa into the cell at −400 kPa, if the membrane permits water movement.
questions.explanation: Compare total water potentials, taking care with negative signs.

remaining: SL and HL material are separately gated. Add solvation, clinical-context applications, uncertainty and error-bar practice, and more tissue-level HL applications.

title: Reproduction

sections.title: Sexual and asexual reproduction
sections.body: Asexual reproduction does not require fusion of gametes and can produce offspring rapidly from one parent. Sexual reproduction combines genetic contributions through gametes and fertilization, creating new combinations of alleles. Meiosis reduces chromosome number and fertilization restores it. The relative advantages depend on conditions: rapid multiplication can be useful in a stable setting, while variation can affect how a population responds to change.
sections.pitfall: Asexually produced descendants are not guaranteed to remain genetically identical forever because mutations can occur.

sections.title: Reproduction in flowering plants
sections.body: Pollination transfers pollen to a receptive stigma; it is distinct from fertilization. A compatible pollen grain can produce a tube through which male gametes reach the ovule. Fertilization produces a zygote that develops into an embryo. A seed protects the embryo and contains or accesses reserves used during germination. Dispersal moves seeds away from the parent, potentially reducing competition and allowing colonization.
sections.pitfall: Pollination transfers pollen; it does not itself describe the fusion of gamete nuclei.

questions.prompt: Which event is pollination?
questions.answer: Transfer of pollen to a receptive stigma
distractors: Fusion of gamete nuclei
Growth of an embryo from a zygote
Movement of a mature seed away from its parent
questions.explanation: Pollination precedes the later events of fertilization, seed development and dispersal.

questions.prompt: Discuss one advantage and one limitation of asexual reproduction in a changing environment.
questions.answer: It can allow rapid reproduction without finding a mate.~Limited initial genetic variation may leave many descendants similarly vulnerable to a new challenge.~The outcome depends on existing variation, mutation and the particular environmental change.
questions.explanation: Consider both a benefit and a relevant limitation without treating either strategy as universally superior.

questions.prompt: A sexually reproducing species has diploid cells with 18 chromosomes. Determine the usual chromosome number in a gamete and in a zygote formed by two normal gametes.
questions.answer: A gamete usually contains 9 chromosomes.~Fusion of two normal gametes restores 18 chromosomes in the zygote.
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the number of chromosome sets and fertilization combines two haploid sets.

remaining: Major gap remains: human reproductive anatomy, menstrual hormonal control, fertilization and IVF, detailed flower diagrams and HL pregnancy and gametogenesis require dedicated resources. This topic is explicitly an overview, not complete revision.

title: Inheritance

sections.title: Alleles, genotype and phenotype
sections.body: Alleles are alternative sequence forms of a gene. A diploid organism usually carries two alleles at an autosomal locus, one inherited from each parent. Homozygous means the alleles are the same; heterozygous means they differ. Genotype describes genetic constitution, while phenotype describes observable characteristics influenced by genotype and environment. Under complete dominance, a heterozygote has the dominant phenotype; dominance does not imply that an allele is common or beneficial.
sections.pitfall: Dominant does not mean more frequent, stronger or more adaptive.

sections.title: Predicting inheritance
sections.body: A Punnett grid combines possible gametes to predict genotype probabilities under stated assumptions. For Aa × Aa with equal segregation, the expected genotype proportions are 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa and 1/4 aa. With complete dominance and full penetrance, the expected phenotype ratio is 3:1. These are probabilities over repeated outcomes, not a promise that every family of four contains exactly those phenotypes. Independent events do not remember the outcomes of previous births.
sections.pitfall: An expected genetic ratio is not an exact requirement for each small group of offspring.

questions.prompt: What does heterozygous mean at a specified diploid locus?
questions.answer: The two alleles differ
distractors: Both alleles are necessarily dominant
Both alleles are identical
The organism has only one chromosome in total
questions.explanation: Heterozygosity concerns whether the two allele forms at that locus differ.

questions.prompt: Distinguish genotype from phenotype.
questions.answer: Genotype describes genetic constitution, such as the alleles at a locus.~Phenotype describes observable characteristics resulting from genotype and environmental influences.
questions.explanation: An observed characteristic alone may not uniquely identify the underlying genotype.

questions.prompt: In an Aa × Aa cross, calculate the probability that two independently produced offspring are both aa.
questions.answer: The probability of aa for each offspring is 1/4.~For two independent offspring, the probability is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, or 6.25%.
questions.explanation: Multiply independent probabilities; do not add them for the event that both occur.

remaining: Add pedigrees, sex-linked inheritance, codominance and multiple alleles, environmental and polygenic variation, and HL linkage and statistical testing.

title: Homeostasis

sections.title: Homeostasis and negative feedback
sections.body: Homeostasis maintains internal variables within ranges compatible with function despite disturbances. Receptors detect a variable, an integrating system coordinates a response and effectors act. In negative feedback, the response opposes the initial deviation: an excessive rise produces actions that lower the variable, while an excessive fall produces actions that raise it. Regulation does not imply that the variable remains perfectly constant at every moment.
sections.pitfall: Negative feedback means opposition to a deviation, not necessarily a decrease in the variable.

sections.title: Blood-glucose regulation
sections.body: Pancreatic cells respond to blood-glucose changes. When glucose is high, insulin promotes uptake in responsive tissues and storage, including glycogen formation. When glucose falls, glucagon promotes hepatic glucose release, including through glycogen breakdown. These opposing effects help restore the concentration toward a regulated range. Type 1 diabetes involves loss of insulin-producing cells, whereas type 2 commonly involves reduced responsiveness to insulin together with impaired secretion as it progresses.
sections.pitfall: Glucagon is a hormone; glycogen is a carbohydrate store. Similar names do not imply the same substance.

sections.title: Regulating body temperature
sections.body: The hypothalamus integrates temperature information from the body and coordinates effectors. Sweating can increase evaporative heat loss, and increased skin blood flow transfers more heat toward the surface. When cold, reduced skin blood flow conserves heat and shivering increases muscular heat production. Brown adipose tissue can generate heat through uncoupled respiration. Hormonal signals involving the pituitary and thyroid can influence metabolic heat production. Hair erection has limited insulating benefit in humans compared with densely furred mammals.
sections.pitfall: Sweat cools most effectively when it evaporates; liquid simply remaining on the skin does not produce the same heat loss.

sections.title: Kidneys and water balance
sections.body: Ultrafiltration at the glomerulus moves water and small solutes into the nephron while retaining blood cells and most large proteins. Useful solutes are selectively reabsorbed, especially in the proximal convoluted tubule. Salt transport by the ascending limb helps establish a concentrated medulla. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors influence ADH release from the posterior pituitary. ADH promotes aquaporin insertion in collecting-duct cells, increasing water permeability so more water can return to the body along the osmotic gradient.
sections.pitfall: Filtration is not the same as excretion: much of the filtered material is reabsorbed before urine leaves the body.

questions.prompt: Which response illustrates negative feedback after body temperature rises?
questions.answer: Increased evaporative heat loss that tends to lower temperature
distractors: A response that increases heat production further
A response that reinforces the temperature increase
No response until temperature can no longer change
questions.explanation: The response opposes the original deviation rather than amplifying it.

questions.prompt: Compare the effects of insulin and glucagon on blood-glucose regulation.
questions.answer: Insulin promotes processes that lower raised blood glucose, including uptake and storage.~Glucagon promotes hepatic glucose release when blood glucose is low.~Their opposing effects contribute to negative-feedback regulation.
questions.explanation: Link each hormone to the relevant starting condition and direction of response.

questions.prompt: A graph shows glucose rising after a meal and later returning toward its starting range. Does this prove that glucose regulation keeps the concentration exactly constant? Explain.
questions.answer: No: the graph shows a temporary deviation.~Return toward the range is consistent with regulation despite fluctuation, rather than perfect constancy.~The graph alone does not identify every mechanism responsible.
questions.explanation: Homeostasis allows regulated variation and delays in feedback.

questions.prompt: Explain why increased humidity can reduce the cooling effect of sweating.
questions.answer: High humidity reduces the gradient driving evaporation into the surrounding air.~Less evaporation means less heat is removed from the body by that route.
questions.explanation: The relevant process is evaporation, not simply sweat production.

questions.prompt: Explain how increased ADH can reduce water loss in urine.
questions.answer: ADH promotes aquaporin insertion in collecting-duct cell membranes.~Water permeability increases and more water can be reabsorbed into the concentrated surrounding tissues.~Less water remains in the urine.
questions.explanation: Connect hormonal signalling, membrane permeability and the existing osmotic gradient.

remaining: Core feedback, glucose and temperature have teaching and practice. Add full diabetes context, physiological data, kidney diagrams, quantitative osmolality and HL redistribution of blood flow. Numbered references do not certify every requirement within a point.

title: Natural selection

sections.title: Variation and differential reproduction
sections.body: Populations contain variation, some of which is heritable. Organisms generally produce more potential offspring than can all survive and reproduce. In a given environment, some inherited variants contribute to greater reproductive success. Alleles associated with that success can become more frequent over generations. Fitness describes contribution to future generations in context, not simply size, strength or longevity.
sections.pitfall: Individuals are selected, while the inherited composition of the population changes across generations.

sections.title: Selection is environment-dependent
sections.body: An advantage depends on the environment and can change when conditions change. Antibiotic exposure can favour resistant bacterial variants, while resistance may have a cost in a different setting. Artificial selection occurs when humans choose which organisms reproduce according to desired characteristics. It still depends on heritable variation and differential reproduction, although the selecting conditions differ from many natural examples.
sections.pitfall: Selection does not create the required mutation on demand, and evolution has no predetermined goal.

questions.prompt: Which measure is most directly relevant to evolutionary fitness?
questions.answer: Relative contribution of surviving offspring to future generations
distractors: Body mass alone
Age at death regardless of reproduction
The number of traits an observer considers impressive
questions.explanation: Fitness concerns reproductive contribution in the relevant environment.

questions.prompt: Explain how a heritable resistance trait can become more common during repeated antibiotic exposure.
questions.answer: Resistance varies among bacteria and can be inherited.~Exposure reduces the survival or reproduction of susceptible variants more strongly.~Resistant variants contribute a larger share of descendants, increasing the trait's frequency.
questions.explanation: Include existing variation, heritability and differential reproductive success.

questions.prompt: A resistant variant grows more slowly than a susceptible variant without antibiotic but survives better during exposure. Evaluate the claim that resistance is always advantageous.
questions.answer: The advantage depends on the environment.~Resistance benefits survival during exposure but the slower growth can impose a cost without the antibiotic.~Relative reproductive success under each condition determines the selective outcome.
questions.explanation: A trait can have both benefits and costs rather than an unconditional advantage.

remaining: Add required selection examples and HL allele-frequency, equilibrium and selection-pattern applications.

title: Stability and change

sections.title: Ecosystem stability
sections.body: Stability can include resistance to disturbance and recovery afterward. Diversity of interactions, continuing energy inputs and recycling of nutrients can contribute to persistence. A stable ecosystem need not have constant population sizes: seasonal and other fluctuations can occur within a persistent system. Removing a species or changing an abiotic factor can have indirect consequences through food webs and competition.
sections.pitfall: Stability does not mean that nothing changes, or that every diverse ecosystem resists every disturbance equally.

sections.title: Succession and altered conditions
sections.body: Ecological succession is change in community composition over time. Early colonizers can alter conditions by contributing organic matter, modifying soil and changing shade or moisture. Later species establish under the altered conditions. Disturbance can interrupt or redirect this sequence. Predicting one inevitable final community is often too simple because local conditions, dispersal and repeated disturbances affect the pathway.
sections.pitfall: Succession concerns changes in communities, not an individual organism deliberately progressing toward a final form.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly indicates resilience after a disturbance?
questions.answer: The community returns toward its previous functioning over time
distractors: No immediate response to the disturbance
The community never receives energy inputs
Every population remains exactly constant at all times
questions.explanation: Resilience concerns recovery. Resistance concerns how little a system initially changes.

questions.prompt: Explain how early colonizers can influence which species establish later.
questions.answer: They can change conditions such as soil organic matter, nutrient availability or shade.~Those changes alter the conditions encountered by arriving species, favouring some and excluding others.
questions.explanation: Link organism activity to an environmental change and then to establishment.

questions.prompt: A community has similar total biomass before and after disturbance, but half its original species are absent afterward. Evaluate the claim that no important ecological change occurred.
questions.answer: Total biomass is only one property of the community.~Species composition and associated interactions have changed substantially.~Functional measurements and species data are needed alongside biomass to assess stability.
questions.explanation: A stable aggregate can conceal changes in the parts and their interactions.

remaining: Add sustainable-system investigations, detailed succession evidence, required case studies and HL ecosystem change and management.

title: Climate change

sections.title: Energy balance and greenhouse gases
sections.body: Earth receives energy mainly as short-wave solar radiation and emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared radiation, affecting the rate at which energy escapes to space. Increasing their concentration can alter the energy balance and raise the temperature required for balance. Carbon dioxide released from fossil fuels adds carbon from long-term stores to the active atmosphere–ocean–biosphere system. Weather is a short-term state; climate describes patterns over longer intervals.
sections.pitfall: A cold day in one location does not by itself test a trend in global climate.

sections.title: Biological responses and feedback
sections.body: Changing temperature and precipitation can shift species distributions, breeding times and interactions. Species respond at different rates, so the timing of food availability can become mismatched with consumer needs. Loss of reflective ice can increase solar-energy absorption, reinforcing warming. Biological responses also depend on dispersal barriers and other pressures. A correlation between temperature and a biological change is useful evidence, but alternative explanations and mechanisms should be investigated.
sections.pitfall: An observed range shift does not mean every species can move quickly enough to remain in suitable conditions.

questions.prompt: Which interaction is central to the greenhouse effect?
questions.answer: Absorption and emission of infrared radiation by greenhouse gases
distractors: Complete reflection of all sunlight before it reaches Earth
Conversion of carbon dioxide directly into visible sunlight
Permanent storage of all outgoing radiation without re-emission
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases affect infrared energy transfer; they do not simply block every form of radiation.

questions.prompt: Explain how reduced ice cover can produce positive feedback in warming.
questions.answer: Less reflective ice can lower the surface's reflectivity.~More incoming solar energy is absorbed, contributing to further warming.~Additional warming can cause further ice loss.
questions.explanation: Close the feedback loop by showing how the response reinforces the initial change.

questions.prompt: Over several decades, an insect's peak abundance advances by 14 days while a bird's hatching date advances by 3 days. Suggest a possible consequence and one measurement needed to test it.
questions.answer: The timing difference may reduce overlap between chick demand and peak food availability.~Measure food availability during chick rearing and a relevant outcome such as growth or survival.
questions.explanation: The timing data support a hypothesis, not proof of a population decline.

remaining: Add required climate datasets, ocean and ecosystem case studies, mitigation evaluation and HL feedback and change mechanisms. Numerical examples in this pack are exercises rather than live climate observations.
